text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNNondimensionalize hydrostatic balance, integrate from centre to surface, and explain why mass is independent of central density for n = 3. Connect to foundations: The Chandrasekhar mass: a white dwarf’s limit ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01From global balance to a thin shell A global estimate P ∼ GM²/R⁴ treats a star as a whole. Now distinguish the enclosed mass m(r), local pressure P(r), and density ρ(r). Assume a static, spherical, nonrotating object with Newtonian gravity. A shell of thickness Δr has mass about 4πr²ρΔr. Its net outward pressure force is −4πr²ΔP; the inward gravitational force is (Gm/r²)4πr²ρΔr. Balance them and take the thin-shell limit. dPdr = −Gmρr² dmdr = 4πr²ρ dP/dr is the local change in pressure with radius. Its negative sign means pressure decreases outward. The second equation expresses mass conservation as successive shells are added. 02Eliminate mass and close the model Multiply the first equation by r²/ρ to get r²P′/ρ = −Gm. Differentiate with respect to r and use the second equation; here a prime means an r derivative. 1r²ddr (r²ρdPdr) = −4πGρ We still need a pressure–density relation. Adopt a polytropic relation with K and n constant throughout the object. The index n is not a particle count: it specifies the density dependence of pressure. P = Kρ1+1/n (n > 0) This is a structural model, not a universal law with constant K and n for all stars. An isothermal sphere P = cs²ρ requires a different scaling; it is distinct from the finite-n models considered here. 03Remove the units, step by step Let ρc be the central density and use θ(ξ) to describe the profile. The scale a is a length; ξ and θ are dimensionless. Use d/dr = (1/a)d/dξ. ρ = ρcθn, r = aξ P = Kρc1+1/nθn+1 1ρdPdr = (n+1)Kρc1/nadθdξ Substitute into the previous equation. Transforming the outer 1/r² and derivative leaves a factor (n+1)Kρc1/n/a² on the left and 4πGρc on the right. Choose a so that these factors match. a² = (n+1)K4πGρc(1−n)/n 1ξ²ddξ(ξ²dθdξ) = −θn θ″ + 2ξθ′ + θn = 0 The Lane–Emden equation; primes now denote ξ derivatives. 04Start at a regular centre By definition θ(0) = 1. A smooth spherical centre has no preferred direction, so θ′(0) = 0. Direct numerical evaluation at ξ = 0 would nevertheless give 0/0 in 2θ′/ξ. Insert θ = 1 + Aξ² + Bξ⁴ + … . Constant terms give 6A + 1 = 0; ξ² terms give 20B + nA = 0. This supplies starting values just outside the centre. θ = 1 − ξ²6 + nξ⁴120 + … θ′ = −ξ3 + nξ³30 + … Start at a small ε > 0 and integrate outward using two first-order equations, θ′ = q and q′ = −2q/ξ − θⁿ. The first zero ξ₁ defines the surface. Here we consider 0 < n < 5. 05Integrate and compare with a known solution For n = 1, θ = sinξ/ξ is a solution. Differentiating ξ²θ′ = ξcosξ − sinξ gives −ξsinξ = −ξ²θ, as required. The central limit is one and the surface is ξ₁ = π. This provides an independent check on the numerical method. The numerical recipe: fourth-order Runge–Kutta For y′ = F(x,y), y can be a scalar or a vector such as (θ,q). With step h, calculate these four slopes in order. k₁ = F(x,y) k₂ = F(x+h/2, y+hk₁/2) k₃ = F(x+h/2, y+hk₂/2) k₄ = F(x+h, y+hk₃) y(x+h) ≈ y(x) + h6(k₁+2k₂+2k₃+k₄) The panel uses fourth-order Runge–Kutta: evaluate four slopes over a short interval and combine them with weights 1:2:2:1. It starts at ε = 10⁻⁴ and interpolates the surface between neighbouring points. Halve the step to check convergence. 06Turn the dimensionless shape into radius and mass Integrating the equation from centre to surface expresses the density integral through the surface slope. Call this dimensionless mass μₙ. μn ≡ ∫0ξ₁ ξ²θndξ = −ξ₁²θ′(ξ₁) R = aξ₁, M = 4πa³ρcμn R ∝ K1/2ρc(1−n)/(2n) M ∝ K3/2ρc(3−n)/(2n) Scaling along a sequence at fixed n; G is also constant. For n = 3/2, M ∝ ρc1/2 and R ∝ ρc−1/6, giving R ∝ M−1/3 at fixed K. For n = 3, the density exponent in M vanishes: changing radius does not change the equilibrium mass at the same K. 07Recover the Chandrasekhar coefficient In the cold, completely degenerate, ultrarelativistic electron limit, P = KURρ4/3, so n = 3. Quantum statistics supplies KUR below. Here μe is mass per electron in units of the atomic mass constant mu, and ℏ = h/(2π). KUR = ℏc4(3π²)1/3(μemu)−4/3 Numerical integration gives ξ₁ ≈ 6.89685 and μ₃ ≈ 2.01824. Cancel the central density in a³ρc to recover the structural coefficient supplied in the foundation lesson. M = 4πμ₃(KURπG)3/2 MCh ≈ 5.83μe² M☉ ≈ 1.46 M☉ (μe = 2) This is an idealized limiting mass. General relativity, electron capture, Coulomb effects, finite temperature, and rotation are omitted. The n = 3 equilibrium equation alone does not establish dynamical stability. The n = 5 solution has no finite zero; the uniform-density n = 0 model also needs separate treatment. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed K and composition, increase the central density eightfold. How do a, R, and M change for n = 3? What about n = 3/2? Show the answer and reasoning a and R scale as ρc(1−n)/(2n); M scales as ρc(3−n)/(2n). For n = 3, a and R halve while M stays fixed. For n = 3/2, a and R decrease by 1/√2 and M increases by √8. The dimensionless surface ξ₁ and mass μₙ stay fixed because each sequence keeps n and K fixed. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text.
